story851:
In the beginning, before the world had shape or name, only Tawa existed — the Sun Spirit, a being of pure light suspended in Tokpella, the Endless Space. There was no earth, no sky, no water. Only Tawa, burning quietly in the void like a coal that refuses to die.

Tawa formed the First World from his own light, shaping it the way a dreamer shapes a dream. The creatures that lived there were small and insect-like, burrowing in caves beneath a sky that had no sun. They were unhappy in their darkness, whispering to each other about the light they had never seen.

To help them, Tawa created his nephew Sotuknang — a being of structure and purpose. Sotuknang in turn created Spider Woman, Spider Grandmother, as a messenger and helper. She was ancient and wise, with legs like the rays of the dawn and eyes that could see in every direction at once.

Spider Woman gathered the First World creatures and led them to the Second World, where they took on the forms of wolves and bears. Still the world was not right — too wild, too cold, too full of teeth.

They climbed to the Third World, where the creatures finally became human. Spider Woman taught them to weave cloth and shape pottery. Hummingbird — a tiny, reckless being with iridescent wings — stole the fire drill from the fire spirits and brought it to the people. For the first time, they had warmth and cooked food.

But the people grew wicked. They fought. They forgot the prayers. And so the Third World was destroyed — in some versions by flood, in others by fire — and the survivors climbed through a hollow reed into the Fourth World, the world we know.

There they met Masauwu, the Spirit of Death and Earth God, who wore a mask that was both hideous and beautiful. He gave them the land and four sacred tablets — instructions for how to live, where to settle, and what ceremonies to perform. And the Fourth World began.
story852:
The people of the Third World had grown wicked. They stole from each other. They forgot the songs that held the world together. They mocked the spirits and ignored the sacred fires. The sky darkened with their bad deeds, and the ground shook beneath their feet.

Spider Grandmother saw what was happening and wept. She went to Tawa and pleaded: "Save the ones who still have good hearts. Let the wicked face the flood, but spare the kind."

Tawa agreed. At the center of the Third World, where a great spring bubbled up from the earth, Spider Grandmother commanded a hollow bamboo reed to grow. It pushed upward through the ground, through the rock, through the darkness between worlds, until its tip emerged into the Fourth World like a green finger pointing at the sky.

The people gathered around the reed. Spider Grandmother looked at them with old eyes. "Only those who have shown kindness," she said. "Only those who have shared their food, who have helped their neighbors, who have spoken truthfully. The reed will not open for the wicked."

One by one, the good people climbed inside. The reed was narrow, and the climb was long — through three worlds of darkness, past rivers of fire and walls of stone. Some people could not make the journey. The reed rejected them, its walls closing tight around those whose hearts were heavy with cruelty.

At the top, they emerged into the Fourth World through an opening called the sipapu — traditionally located at the Grand Canyon, though different villages claim different locations. They found themselves on a small island in a vast ocean, blinking in light they had never seen.

Masauwu was waiting for them. He wore his terrible mask and carried four tablets. "This is your land," he said. "These are your instructions. Follow them, and you will prosper. Forget them, and you will wander."

The people took the tablets and walked into the Fourth World. Behind them, the sipapu closed. The Third World was gone. But the people carried its memory in their ceremonies, in the songs they sang at dawn, in the prayers they whispered before planting corn.
story853:
In the villages around Oraibi — one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements in North America — the elders tell a different story of how the people came to the Fourth World. This is the flood story.

Tawa saw the wickedness of the Third World and decided to destroy it. But before the destruction, Spider Grandmother chose the righteous and sealed them inside hollow reeds — not the single bamboo of the sipapu story, but many reeds, each one large enough to hold a family.

The flood came from below, not above. The ground opened and water poured in, rising faster than anyone could climb. The reeds floated, bobbing on the surface like cattails on a pond. The people huddled inside, listening to the Third World drown beneath them.

For days they floated. The water was endless in every direction — no land, no mountains, no landmark of any kind. The people grew afraid. "We will starve," they said. "There is nothing to eat on the water."

Spider Grandmother told them to make boats from more reeds. They wove the reeds into rafts and sailed east, using the position of the sun to guide them. They stopped at islands that rose from the water — stepping-stones of rock and sand — and rested before continuing.

The Hopi Water Clan's name, Patkinyamu, means 'dwelling-on-water,' preserving the memory of this ocean voyage in their very identity.

After many days, the mountains of the Fourth World rose from the water like the backs of sleeping giants. The people climbed ashore, exhausted and sunburned, and collapsed on the rocky coast. They had nothing — no tools, no food, no shelter. Spider Grandmother taught them to make boats from the reeds they still carried, to fish with sharpened sticks, to build shelters from driftwood.

The sipapu story and the flood story are both told. Different villages emphasize different versions. But both agree on this: the people who reached the Fourth World were chosen for their goodness, and they were given a second chance.
story854:
When the Hopi first arrived in the Fourth World, they were one people — speaking one language, following one set of customs. But the land was vast, and Masauwu had given them four tablets with instructions to explore, to settle, and to remember.

The clans divided. Some went north, some south, some east, some west. They carried with them the knowledge Spider Grandmother had given them — how to plant corn, how to build houses, how to perform ceremonies. They left symbols on rocks as they traveled, marking their passage the way a bird marks its path through the sky.

Clans were named after events or signs. The Corn Clan was named because they found a field of corn growing wild. The Bear Clan was named because a bear led them to water. The Firewood Clan was named because they gathered the best firewood. Each name carried a story, and each story carried a lesson.

Periods of harmony alternated with wickedness, contention, and separation — a pattern that had begun in the First World and would repeat through every world. Some clans stopped migrating and built towns, only to abandon them when the springs dried up or the soil grew thin.

Far to the north was the Back Door — possibly the Bering land bridge — through which other peoples had entered the Fourth World. But this door was closed to the Hopi. Their path was different. Their destination was specific.

Masauwu guided them. He appeared at crossroads and on mountaintops, wearing his mask of death and life. "Go east," he told one clan. "Go south," he told another. "Go to the place where three mesas stand like prayer sticks pointing at the sky."

Eventually, the clans converged in northeastern Arizona, on the three mesas that Masauwu had promised. They built their towns — Walpi on First Mesa, Shongopavi and Oraibi on Second and Third Mesa — and planted their corn in the dry soil. The migrations were over. The Hopi were home.

But the stories of the journey are preserved in their dances, their songs, and the petroglyphs that still mark the rocks across the Southwest — a map of wandering written in stone.
story855:
The drought lasted twelve years. The springs dried to mud. The corn withered in the fields, its leaves curling brown in the relentless sun. Children cried from hunger, and the elders whispered that the Kachinas had abandoned them.

But the Kachinas had not abandoned them. They were watching from the San Francisco Peaks — Nuvatukya'ovi — the sacred mountains north of the villages, hidden in clouds that refused to rain.

One evening, a young girl heard singing coming from the direction of the peaks. She told her grandmother, who told the chief, who gathered the people. They listened. The singing was beautiful, rising and falling like water flowing over stones.

They followed the sound to the base of the mountains and found the Kachinas — ancestral spirits, supernatural beings who had lived in the peaks since the beginning of the Fourth World. The Kachinas agreed to return with the people to their villages.

They came in a great procession. The Kachinas wore masks of every kind — parrot and eagle, deer and bear, sun and moon. They danced in the plazas, their feet stamping the dry earth, their songs calling to the rain spirits. And the rain came.

The Kachinas taught the people agriculture — not just how to plant corn, but how to read the clouds, how to read the soil, how to know when the sun was right and when the frost was done. They taught the ceremonies that would bring rain each year — the dances, the songs, the prayers that are not merely requests but negotiations with the forces of the sky.

For six months each year, from winter solstice to July, the Kachina spirits live in the Hopi villages. Men who put on the masks do not merely represent the Kachinas — they become them. The mask is not a costume but a face that transforms the wearer into something more than human.

In late July, the Niman — the Homegoing ceremony — marks the Kachinas' return to the mountains. The people watch them go, knowing they will return when the winter solstice turns the year, bringing rain and blessings once more.
story856:
At old Mishongnovi, on Second Mesa, there lived a maiden who refused every suitor. She was proud and beautiful, and she wanted nothing to do with the young men of her village, who were, in her opinion, unremarkable.

One day, a Kachina youth from the San Francisco Peaks saw her and fell in love. He traveled to Mishongnovi by rainbow — stepping from one color to the next until he stood at the edge of the village. He courted her with gifts of turquoise and feathers, with songs that made the corn grow taller just by hearing them.

The maiden agreed to go with him. He led her across the desert to Palotsmo — Sunset Crater — where the Kana-a Kachinas lived in a village of red stone.

But first, she had to prove herself. The Kachinas placed her in the kiva — the ceremonial chamber — and left her there for four nights. Each night, the North Wind entered the kiva and tried to freeze her. The first night, the cold was bitter. The second night, it was unbearable. The third night, the maiden's breath turned to ice crystals. But she held firm, wrapped in the songs her mother had taught her, and the North Wind could not break her.

On the fourth night, she emerged from the kiva, transformed. The Kana-a Kachinas accepted her as one of their own. She married the youth and lived among them.

But back in Mishongnovi, a wicked man had heard of the maiden's journey. He disguised himself as the Kachina husband and deceived the people, causing harm that echoed through the village.

The Kana-a Kachinas at Sunset Crater took pity on the people suffering from this deception. They gathered sweet corn and food, and in a great procession they danced through the streets of Mishongnovi. At each house, they asked the people to leave an ear of corn in their empty storage room. When the people awoke the next morning, their storage rooms were miraculously full of corn.

The Kana-a Kachinas then entered a small butte near the village, which remains their home to this day. The people of Mishongnovi leave offerings at its base, remembering the gift of corn and the lesson that even deception cannot long obscure the truth.
story857:
In Walpi, on First Mesa, an old Ahö'li Kachina lived with his sister, the Kachin-mana. He was so old and frail that his sister led him by the hand wherever he went. They planted in their field south of the mesa, and at each corner they placed a báho — a small prayer offering of woven cotton and feathers.

Meanwhile, above them in the kivas, the great Kachinas were preparing. The Ââ'ototo, Big-Horn Kachina, led a procession down the mesa, marking shrines between the villages with sacred objects.

As they descended into the valley, they encountered the Cóoyoko — a dangerous being with protruding eyes, a large knife, and rattles of bone and shell around his body. The Cóoyoko killed and devoured children who wandered too far from the village.

The Kachinas negotiated with the Cóoyoko. "Let us pass," they said. "We will bring rain to the fields. In return, you may destroy only the bad — the wicked and the cruel."

The Cóoyoko agreed. The Kachinas continued into the valley, where they found a beautiful house hidden in the cottonwood trees. They entered and sang all night — songs of rain, songs of growth, songs of the earth opening to receive the sky's gift.

By morning, rain poured from clouds that had not been there the night before. The dry arroyos filled. The fields drank deeply. By noon, the sun broke through, and the Kachinas emerged from the house to find their fields filled with corn, melons, and squashes — all growing at supernatural speed, as if the earth were making up for twelve years of drought in a single morning.

Big-Skeleton — Wokómásauwuu — who owns the earth and all that grows upon it, met the Kachinas as they climbed back toward the mesa. "You have done well," he said. "But you must live on top of the mesa, not in the valley. The valley is for growing. The mesa is for watching."

And so Walpi was built on the very top of First Mesa, where the Kachinas could look down upon their fields and the people could look up at the sky.
story858:
A maiden in the village was grinding corn in her lodge, the rhythmic sound of the metate filling the room like a heartbeat, when the Póngo — Circle Kachina — appeared at her door. He had been dancing at the kivas around the village, his round mask painted with the symbols of the four directions, his body wrapped in fine white cotton.

He danced for her — a courtship dance, his feet stamping the hard-packed floor, his arms spreading like wings. She smiled. She agreed to marry him.

She went to the Kachina kiva, where many different Kachinas gathered — Crow Mother, the Parrot Kachinas, the warrior Kachinas — all preparing for the spring dances. She cooked their food while they wove her bridal costume: a robe of white turkey feathers, a belt of turquoise beads, moccasins of soft deerskin.

They had two children, both Circle Kachinas — small, round-faced beings who danced in the plazas with their father.

But the Hotóto Kachina — a being of great charm and questionable intentions — seduced the wife away to Shongópavi, another village on Second Mesa. The Circle Kachina followed her tracks across the mesa, carrying his children on his back.

At the kiva in Shongópavi, the Flute priests played for four days. The music was so beautiful that the water spirits wept, and their tears formed a pool at the kiva's entrance. On the fourth day, the wife emerged from the water in her bridal costume, restored.

The Flute priests declared: "You shall always follow each other this way."

The two ran westward. They are still running. They became the stars that chase each other across the sky — Nangö'sohu — one constantly overtaking and then falling behind the other. In the Hopi sky, you can see them every night: two points of light, forever pursuing, forever separated, forever connected.
story859:
In Oraibi, on Third Mesa, the Snow Kachinas were practicing for a dance in the Chórzhovi kiva. Their masks were white as the first frost, and their songs were the songs of winter — slow, deep, resonant with the weight of snow.

North of the village, at a place called Katcínavala, lived Toad Woman with her son. The boy was small and strange — his skin bumpy, his eyes too large, his manner quiet. He liked ants. He would sit for hours watching them carry seeds across the sand, marveling at their industry.

Every day, the boy crept to the kiva and pressed his ear against the stone wall, listening to the Kachinas sing. The music moved him in ways he could not explain. His feet tapped. His hands waved. He wanted to dance.

On the day of the dance, the Toad Boy painted his face with red ochre and wore a wildcat robe over his small, bumpy body. He walked to the plaza and stood among the children.

The children laughed at him. "Look at the Toad Boy!" they cried. "He thinks he can dance!" They grabbed him and carried him to an anthill, dumping him on top of it because he liked ants.

The boy sat on the anthill and ate the ants, one by one, while the dance continued. When the Kachinas finished, they gave the children red piki — thin, paper-like bread made from blue corn. The Toad Boy received a piece. He carried it home to his mother.

She was happy. They ate it together in their small lodge, the sweet, thin bread dissolving on their tongues.

This story teaches a Hopi value that runs deeper than it appears: inclusion. Even the lowliest creature — a toad boy who eats ants — has a place in the Kachina celebrations. The dance is not for the beautiful or the strong. It is for everyone. And the gift of piki, that thin red bread, is the gift of community itself.
story860:
In the time before the stars were placed, the sky was a blank canvas of darkness, and the animals were given the task of decorating it.

The Beaver went first. He was careful and methodical, placing each star in a straight line, like the logs of a dam. The Deer followed, arranging stars in gentle arcs that mirrored the paths she walked through the forest. The Eagle placed the brightest stars in patterns that resembled wings spread against the night.

Coyote watched. He had been given the task of placing the scattered stars — the ones that did not fit into any pattern, the ones that were too small or too dim for the important constellations.

The work was slow. Each animal placed a star, then stepped back to admire it, then placed another. The night was cold and the work was tedious. Coyote grew impatient.

"This is taking too long," he said. "Let me help."

The other animals were wary, but they gave him a blanket full of stars — hundreds of them, glowing faintly like embers. Coyote grabbed the blanket and flung it into the sky.

Stars scattered in every direction. Some landed in neat rows. Others landed in clumps. Some landed alone, isolated in vast dark spaces. The careful patterns the other animals had created were disrupted, overlaid with Coyote's chaotic scatter.

The animals were angry. "You've ruined it!" the Beaver cried.

But the Creator looked at the sky and saw something the animals did not. The orderly patterns — the Big Dipper, the Hunter, the Pleiades — told stories and marked seasons. But Coyote's scattered stars filled the spaces between, creating the Milky Way and the countless faint lights that make the night sky feel infinite.

"Both are necessary," the Creator said. "Order without chaos is a cage. Chaos without order is a flood. Together, they are the sky."

And so the night remains: partly patterned, partly scattered, partly deliberate, partly accidental — like the world itself.
story861:
The boy's name has been lost, which is fitting, because the story is not about who he was but about what he found. He lived in a village on the mesas, a quiet boy with restless feet and a mind that wandered beyond the horizon.

One morning, he left. He told no one where he was going. He walked east, toward the rising sun, carrying nothing but a water gourd and a piece of dried corn.

He walked for many days. The mesas gave way to valleys, the valleys to plains, the plains to mountains he had never seen. He crossed rivers too wide to see the other side and climbed passes where the air was thin enough to make him dizzy.

Guided by Spider Grandmother — who appeared to him as an old woman sitting by a fire — he found his way to a body of water so vast it might have been the edge of the world. On the other side, he could see mountains glowing with a light that was not sunlight.

Spider Grandmother taught him to build a boat from reeds and to navigate by the stars. He crossed the water and found a land where spirits lived in houses of cloud and spoke in songs. They taught him sacred ceremonies — dances that brought rain, songs that healed the sick, prayers that opened the way between the living and the dead.

He stayed for one year, learning everything the spirits could teach. When he returned to his people, he brought new dances, new songs, and new knowledge of agriculture — how to read the stars to know when to plant, how to read the clouds to know when rain was coming.

The people benefited from his journey. The corn grew taller. The children grew stronger. The ceremonies became richer.

The boy — for he was still a boy, though his eyes were old — never spoke about where he had been. But sometimes, at night, he would sit outside his lodge and look east, toward the water he had crossed, and the people knew that the knowledge he carried had come from a place beyond the ordinary world.
story862:
Coyote and Bull Snake were friends — an unlikely pair, for Coyote was loud and restless while Bull Snake was quiet and still. But friendship, like rain, falls where it will.

Coyote visited Bull Snake first. He found the burrow beautiful — cool and dark, with walls that glowed faintly with embedded crystals. Bull Snake offered Coyote the best sleeping spot, the one near the back where the air was warmest.

"Now you must visit my den," Coyote said.

Bull Snake agreed and traveled to Coyote's home — a hollow under a rock, messy with old bones and scattered fur. Bull Snake was polite, though the smell was terrible.

During the visit, Coyote decided to play a trick. He told Bull Snake that the greatest honor in his den was to sleep in the deepest corner, where the air was thinnest. Bull Snake, trusting his friend, slithered into the deepest part of the den — and found himself stuck, his thick body wedged between two rocks.

Coyote laughed. "I've caught a snake!" he cried.

But Bull Snake did not laugh. He spoke quietly: "A friend who tricks his guest is no friend at all."

Coyote's laughter died. He helped Bull Snake out of the crevice, cleaning the dirt from his scales with his own paws. "I am sorry," he said, and for once, he meant it.

Bull Snake returned to his own burrow, and Coyote did not visit for a long time. When he finally did, he brought a gift — a fine piece of turquoise, smoothed by the river. Bull Snake accepted it, and the friendship resumed, though it was changed.

The story teaches Hopi values about hospitality and the responsibilities of hosts. A guest must be treated with respect, and a host who betrays that trust loses something that cannot be easily regained.
story863:
Salt was once close to the Hopi villages. It lay in deposits along the riverbanks, white and crystalline, easy to gather. The people used it freely — sprinkling it on corn, preserving meat, marking the boundaries of their fields. They did not think about where it came from or how blessed they were to have it.

Salt Woman saw this. She was a spirit — old and powerful, her body made of the same white crystal as the salt itself. She lived in the deposits, and the people's carelessness wounded her. They wasted salt. They used it in ways that were not sacred. They forgot to give thanks.

One night, Salt Woman packed her belongings — which were also salt — and walked away from the villages. She walked south, toward the Grand Canyon, where the river carved through layers of ancient rock. She walked to other places too — to distant salt flats and underground deposits.

When the people went to gather salt the next morning, the riverbanks were bare. The deposits were gone. They searched everywhere and found nothing.

A hunter tracked Salt Woman's footprints to the Grand Canyon. There he found her, sitting on a ledge overlooking the river. "Come back," he begged. "We need the salt."

Salt Woman looked at him with eyes like white stone. "You forgot to give thanks," she said. "You forgot that the salt is a gift, not a right. If you want salt, you will have to come and get it — the long way, the hard way, so that you remember."

The hunter returned to his people with Salt Woman's words. And so the Hopi began their long journeys to gather salt — traveling for days to the Grand Canyon and other distant locations, carrying the salt back on their backs.

The journey itself became sacred. The people sang songs as they walked. They left offerings at every spring and shrine along the way. And when they returned with the white crystals, they gave thanks — not just for the salt, but for the reminder that blessings must never be taken for granted.
story864:
When a Hopi dies, the journey begins at the sipapu — the opening in the Grand Canyon where the people first entered the Fourth World. The spirit descends through this passage, back through the layers of the earth, following the path that the ancestors once climbed.

But the journey is not a straight descent. The spirit travels westward, following the path of the setting sun, moving through a landscape that is both familiar and strange — a shadow version of the living world, where the rivers flow backward and the mountains lean in directions that make no sense.

Along the way, the spirit encounters challenges. There are crossings where the bridge is made of a single hair, and the spirit must be light enough to walk it. There are gates guarded by spirits who ask questions that only the properly instructed can answer. There are tests of character — moments where the spirit must prove that it lived well, that it honored the ceremonies, that it treated others with respect.

The spirit is judged by Masauwu and the Kachinas. Those who lived well pass into a land of plenty — a world like the Fourth World but better, where the corn grows tall and the water flows clear. Those who lived badly face difficulties — not punishment, but the consequences of their choices, a world shaped by their own failures.

The dead eventually become cloud people. They rise from the land of the dead into the sky, where they join the Kachinas at the San Francisco Peaks. From there, they can bring rain to their living descendants. The dead are not gone — they are transformed, becoming part of the forces that sustain the living world.

This is why the Hopi perform ceremonies for the dead. They pray not for the dead to return, but for the dead to find their place among the cloud people, where they can fulfill their final duty: bringing rain to the fields that feed their children and their children's children.
story865:
In the time after the emergence, when the people first spread across the Fourth World, they all spoke the same language. Every clan, every village, every family — the words flowed between them like water between connected springs.

Mockingbird saw this and was troubled. "The world is too large for one language," he said. "If everyone speaks the same words, they will never be truly different. They will never have their own songs, their own stories, their own way of seeing the world."

Mockingbird had been given a special gift by the Creator: the ability to imitate any sound, any voice, any song. He could sound like a hawk or a frog, like wind in the pines or water over stones. This gift made him the natural choice for what needed to be done.

He called the people together at the base of a great mesa. They gathered in hundreds, their voices rising in a single chorus of the common tongue. Mockingbird perched on a rock above them and began to sing.

He sang the song of the Hawk, and the people of the north spoke in sharp, clipped tones. He sang the song of the Frog, and the people of the south spoke in deep, resonant voices. He sang the song of the Wind, and the people of the east spoke in words that moved quickly, like grass bending in a breeze. He sang the song of the River, and the people of the west spoke in words that flowed slowly and steadily.

He gave each group its own language, its own dialect, its own way of forming words. The people tried to speak to each other and found they could not understand. They laughed. They wept. They gestured. And slowly, they learned to communicate through other means — through sign language, through shared work, through the universal language of ceremony.

Mockingbird also gave the bird species their distinctive calls. The hawk's cry, the owl's hoot, the sparrow's chirp — all are fragments of the languages Mockingbird distributed.

This is why Mockingbird can still mimic other birds and why there are so many different languages among the peoples of the earth. It is not a curse but a gift — the gift of difference, of perspective, of the understanding that the world is too vast to be spoken in a single voice.
